card.title: Part one checkpoint
card.blurb: A short quiz to lock in Part one and earn your XP: what a program is, how it runs, many at once, bits and bytes, and the operating system.
hero.title: Part one checkpoint
intro.0: A short checkpoint before you move on. Answer a handful of questions on Part one - what a program is, how it runs, and what data is made of - to lock it in and earn your XP.
quiz.title: Part one checkpoint
quiz.intro: Seven questions drawn from Part one - the machine. Pick the best answer for each, then submit. Score five or more to pass and earn XP; a fresh set is drawn each time you retry.
question.1.stem: You double-click an app and it starts. In computing terms, what did you just ask the CPU to begin running?
question.1.option.1: A single number held in memory
question.1.option.2: The window that gets drawn on screen
question.1.why: A program is an ordered list of instructions; starting it hands that list to the CPU to run one step at a time.
question.2.stem: A single CPU core is described as doing 'one thing at a time'. What does that actually mean?
question.2.option.0: It runs one instruction, then the next, extremely fast
question.2.option.1: It can run only one program for the whole session
question.2.option.2: It runs one instruction and then waits for the screen
question.2.option.3: It does one calculation per second
question.2.why: A core executes instructions one after another, just very quickly - that speed is what makes it feel like everything happens together.
question.3.stem: On a single-core laptop, a browser and a music player seem to run at the same moment. How is that possible?
question.3.option.0: The operating system switches between them thousands of times a second
question.3.option.1: Each program is given its own core
question.3.option.2: The core runs both programs' instructions simultaneously
question.3.option.3: The screen is split so each gets half
question.3.why: With one core they take turns; the OS time-shares it between processes fast enough to feel simultaneous.
question.4.stem: Your machine has four cores instead of one. What does that let it do that a single core cannot?
question.4.option.0: Run several programs at the very same instant
question.4.option.2: Keep a program running after you close it
question.4.why: Extra cores allow real parallelism - different programs (or parts of one) run at the same instant, not just fast turn-taking.
question.5.stem: Everything a computer stores is built from bits. What is a single bit?
question.5.option.0: A value that is either 0 or 1
question.5.why: A bit is the smallest piece of data - one on/off value, 0 or 1. Larger things are just groups of bits.
question.6.stem: One byte is a group of eight bits. How many different values can a single byte represent?
question.6.why: Eight bits give 2 to the power 8 = 256 combinations - enough for one letter, which is why sizes are measured in bytes.
question.7.stem: A photo has no numbers you can see, yet the computer stores it as numbers. How does that work?
question.7.option.0: Each pixel's colour is recorded as numbers, such as red, green and blue amounts
question.7.option.1: The photo is stored as a sentence describing it
question.7.option.2: The screen makes the numbers up as it draws
question.7.option.3: Only text can become numbers, not images
question.7.why: An image is a grid of pixels, and each pixel's colour is written as numbers - so the whole picture is just numbers.
question.8.stem: When you save your work, it becomes a file. Underneath, what is a file?
question.8.option.0: A named bundle of bytes kept on storage
question.8.option.1: A program that is currently running
question.8.option.2: A single instruction for the CPU
question.8.why: A file is just a named collection of bytes stored on disk; the name lets you and the OS find it again later.
question.9.stem: You save a document and it lands neatly in a folder rather than as raw disk sectors. What arranges that for you?
question.9.option.3: A single variable in the program
question.9.why: The operating system turns raw storage into named files and folders and stands between programs and the hardware.
